extracted.intended_audience: regulators, policymakers, stakeholders and commenters on EPA greenhouse gas endangerment determinations (e.g., government lawyers, industry groups, environmental advocates)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and findings used by the Administrator to determine whether well-mixed greenhouse gas emissions from new motor vehicles cause or contribute to air pollution that may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health and welfare. Covers sectoral evidence, definition of the air pollutant, and the methodology for a cause-or-contribute determination for CAA section 202(a) source categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall endangerment to public welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator considered how elevated concentrations of the well-mixed greenhouse gases and associated climate change affect public welfare by evaluating numerous and far-ranging risks to food production and agriculture, forestry, water resources, sea level rise and coastal areas, energy, infrastructure, and settlements, and ecosystems and wildlife. For each of these sectors, the evidence provides support for a finding of endangerment to public welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate broad, cross-sectoral evidence (scientific literature and assessment reports) regarding current and projected impacts; weigh the clearest and strongest evidence (e.g., water resources and coastal impacts) while also considering other sectors. Recognize that risks and severity of adverse impacts are expected to increase over time with accumulating greenhouse gas concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water resources impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate change threatens availability and quality of water supplies: groundwater recharge may decrease in already stressed regions; coastal salinization from intrusion of salt water; higher water temperatures, increased precipitation intensity, and longer low-flow periods exacerbate many forms of water pollution; pollutants of concern include sediment, nutrients, organic matter, pathogens, pesticides, salt, and thermal pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regional variability in groundwater impacts, vulnerability of island and coastal systems, risks from floods and droughts, and impacts on aquatic ecosystems. Use IPCC and assessment literature confidence language (e.g., 'high confidence') when characterizing risks. Consider implications for public welfare via drinking water supply, ecosystem services, and increased treatment/operating costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea level rise and coastal area risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea level is rising along much of the U.S. coast and will very likely increase, exacerbating progressive inundation, storm-surge flooding, and shoreline erosion. Coastal wetland loss and increased storm surge height pose serious risks; storm-surge and flooding are the most serious risks to coastal areas from sea level rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate location-specific vulnerability (e.g., Atlantic and Gulf Coasts, Pacific Islands, parts of Alaska, urban centers like New Orleans, Miami, NYC). Consider storm-surge interaction with sea level rise (elevated base for surges), potential shortening of 100-year flood return periods (example projections provided), and coastal habitat loss. Account for both observed sea level rise and projections of storm intensity and surge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy, infrastructure, and settlements impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperature increases will change heating and cooling demand and are expected to call for increased electricity production, especially to meet peak demand. Energy sector vulnerabilities include reliance on water for cooling and hydropower. Infrastructure is mainly vulnerable to extreme weather events and to permafrost thaw in Alaska causing soil subsidence affecting pipelines, transmission towers, roads, and water systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both direct losses from events (e.g., equipment damage from flooding) and indirect costs (e.g., raising assets). Consider cascading/interconnected infrastructure failures and geography-linked vulnerabilities (coastal, riverine, climate-sensitive-resource-dependent economies). Include water infrastructure (drinking/wastewater/stormwater) vulnerabilities to flooding, sea level rise, storm surge, low flows, and salt intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecosystems and wildlife impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate change is exerting major influences on natural environments and biodiversity: shifts in habitat ranges, timing of migration and reproduction, and changes in ecosystem structure and functioning. With global warming greater than 2–3 °C, substantial changes in terrestrial ecosystems are very likely with predominantly negative consequences for biodiversity and ecosystem services; many species face increased extinction risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use assessment literature (IPCC) confidence statements; consider species- and ecosystem-specific vulnerabilities (corals, Arctic species, salt marshes, mangroves). Evaluate disturbance regime changes (wildfires, insect outbreaks), range shifts, and interactions with habitat fragmentation and invasive species. Consider both near-term and long-term trajectories of ecosystem service provisioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food production and agriculture impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is potential for near-term crop benefits from increased CO2 and temperature in some regions, but uncertainty exists about realization of benefits given adverse impacts such as extreme weather events, pests, and changes in water availability. Over time, evidence points toward increasing risk of net adverse impacts on U.S. food production and agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance documented CO2 fertilization effects against vulnerabilities from increased climate variability, drought frequency/severity, pests, and water limitations. Consider market-wide effects and regional heterogeneity; treat near-term localized benefits cautiously in light of projected long-term risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forestry impacts and wildfire risk
rubrics_metrics.description: While elevated CO2 and warmer temperatures may increase forest growth in some regions near-term, these benefits are offset by increased wildfire risk, pests, and disease; large, stand-replacing wildfires are likely to increase in frequency over the next several decades due to climate warming and associated aridity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both direct productivity effects and amplified disturbance regimes. Evaluate multi-factor stresses (wildfire, pests, drought) and their potential to overwhelm productivity gains. Use multiple lines of evidence from climate modeling and observational studies to assess wildfire frequency/intensity changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerable populations within settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Within settlements experiencing climate stressors, certain parts of the population may be especially vulnerable: the poor, the elderly, the very young, those already in poor health, the disabled, those living alone, and/or indigenous populations dependent on few resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify demographic and socioeconomic vulnerability factors when assessing welfare impacts. Pay attention to indigenous communities (e.g., Alaska) facing cultural and livelihood disruptions. Factor differential adaptive capacity and resilience in welfare assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts in other world regions that affect the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate change impacts in other regions may in turn affect U.S. public welfare via humanitarian, trade, and national security issues. The IPCC identifies the Arctic, Africa (especially sub-Saharan), small islands, and Asian mega-deltas as especially vulnerable regions that could present risks to the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include international spillover risks (migration, trade disruption, security concerns) as supporting evidence in endangerment assessments. Recognize these risks may not lend themselves to precise projections but are relevant and prudent to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of public comments claiming benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Public commenters noted anticipated benefits of increasing CO2 and temperatures for crops and forest productivity. The Administrator acknowledges positive plant responses but considers that increasing climate variability and other stresses (pests, water limits) may overwhelm benefits over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to comments claiming benefits, acknowledge documented positive responses (CO2 fertilization) but weigh them against assessment literature indicating increased vulnerability, variability, and interacting stresses. Refer to Response to Comments documents and assessment literature for detailed rebuttals and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'air pollution' vs 'air pollutant' and scope of the pollutant
rubrics_metrics.description: For the endangerment finding, 'air pollution' is the total, cumulative stock in the atmosphere (concentration), while the 'air pollutant' is the flow (emissions) changing the size of that stock. The Administrator defines the air pollutant as the aggregate group of six well-mixed greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, and sulfur hexafluoride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the combined grouping of well-mixed greenhouse gases as a single air pollutant for purposes of the cause-or-contribute determination. Use the stock/flow conceptual distinction to link emissions (flow) to atmospheric concentrations (stock) and associated welfare impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for grouping gases as a single well-mixed greenhouse gas pollutant
rubrics_metrics.description: Gases grouped must be directly emitted (not formed through secondary atmospheric processes), sufficiently long-lived to become well mixed globally, exert a climate warming effect by trapping outgoing infrared heat, and have a well-understood radiative forcing effect. Currently only the six named gases meet these criteria, but others may be added if they meet the same criteria in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these technical attributes when determining which substances can reasonably be grouped as a single air pollutant. Document and justify grouping with reference to scientific understanding (longevity, mixing, radiative forcing) and relevant international practices (UNFCCC focus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause-or-contribute finding methodology (use of emissions as proxy)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses emissions as a proxy for contributions to atmospheric concentrations for well-mixed greenhouse gases because cumulative emissions drive cumulative concentration changes; annual emissions are a reasonable proxy for annual incremental changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single statutory approach is required; make a reasoned overall comparison of emissions from the source category to emissions from other sources (both global and national). Use historical emissions data (e.g., 1990–2007) and compare shares (example: ~4% of global greenhouse gas emissions and just over 23% of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions attributable to CAA section 202(a) source categories) to support contribution findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of source categories for CAA section 202(a) cause-or-contribute finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant mobile sources under CAA section 202(a)(1) are 'any class or classes of new motor vehicles or new motor vehicle engines.' The CAA section 202(a) source categories addressed are: passenger cars, light-duty trucks, motorcycles, buses, and medium- and heavy-duty trucks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include emissions from all listed source categories in the contribution determination. When prior determinations focused on subsets, this final finding considers all section 202(a) categories together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative contribution comparisons to establish 'contribute' determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator focused on comparing emissions of CAA section 202(a) source categories relative to both global greenhouse gas emissions and U.S. greenhouse gas emissions. Both comparisons, independently and together, support a finding that these source categories contribute to air pollution that may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health and welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place primary weight on one comparison approach; instead, use multiple comparative perspectives (global and national shares) to reach a reasoned judgment. Cite empirical emission-share figures to substantiate the contribution conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on assessment literature and confidence qualifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator relies on assessment literature (e.g., IPCC) with stated confidence levels (e.g., 'high confidence') to characterize the strength of scientific conclusions about impacts such as water quality exacerbation, ecosystem changes, and other risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In documenting findings, use explicit confidence language drawn from assessment literature to communicate the degree of certainty. Use multiple lines of evidence from assessments and peer-reviewed studies to support conclusions.
